architectural_implications.after: Policy is an externally authored, versioned artifact loaded by the runtime; the execution engine is stable while rules change.
architectural_implications.before: Rules and guardrails are embedded in agent prompts and orchestration code; any rule change is a deploy.
architectural_implications.consequence: Rule changes ship at product speed, compliance diffs become reviewable artifacts, and the runtime must be built to handle policy versions and provenance at invocation time.
architectural_implications.observation: Policy authorship is separated from execution timing (build-state vs run-state).

architectural_implications.after: Explicit DAG/DCG with named nodes, edges, parallel branches, and exception paths, executed by a graph engine.
architectural_implications.before: Linear pipelines or ad-hoc prompt chains; iteration hidden inside a single agent call or faked by re-running the pipeline.
architectural_implications.consequence: Parallel human reviews and bottleneck visibility become possible, but the engine must support loop bounds, per-node state, and trace capture across cycles.
architectural_implications.observation: Workflows are modeled as directed graphs, including cyclic ones for refine loops.

architectural_implications.after: Review routing is a policy-threshold function of a measured confidence metric; oversight degrades smoothly from 100% to sampling to exceptions-only.
architectural_implications.before: Human-in-the-loop is a boolean switch or an escalation triggered by ad-hoc heuristics.
architectural_implications.consequence: The eval/confidence pipeline becomes production-critical infrastructure — its availability and calibration directly determine operational risk, not just reporting quality.
architectural_implications.observation: The confidence score gates the human review fraction.

architectural_implications.after: Runtime traces feed the representative dataset used for statistical evals, closing a loop between production behavior and the confidence metric.
architectural_implications.before: Logs and traces are retained for incident forensics; test coverage is authored separately as fixtures.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires trace schema discipline, PII/redaction policy on eval data, and versioning of datasets so confidence comparisons across time stay valid.
architectural_implications.observation: Traces become eval inputs, not just debugging artifacts.

article_ideas.angle: Take the audience's instinct that 'adding a confidence score' is a reporting feature and invert it: show the engineering obligations (calibration, monitoring, rollback) that follow the moment the score gates review routing.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and applied-AI engineers building human-in-the-loop systems, plus engineering managers who own the review headcount
article_ideas.based_on: The confidence metric is an operational control input
article_ideas.thesis: Once a confidence threshold decides how many outputs a human actually inspects, the scorer stops being reporting infrastructure and becomes the component that sets operational risk. Teams must treat it accordingly: calibration harnesses, drift detection, per-node reliability diagrams, and an automated path back down the autonomy ladder — because the failure mode of a miscalibrated scorer is invisible by construction once oversight is exception-only.
article_ideas.title: Your Confidence Score Is a Control Plane, Not a Dashboard Number

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the build-state/run-state split as a release-engineering argument rather than a governance argument, with the reviewer's diff as the deliverable.
article_ideas.audience: Enterprise architects, compliance-adjacent engineering leads, platform teams shipping regulated workflows
article_ideas.based_on: Policy is a versioned artifact owned outside the runtime
article_ideas.thesis: Embedding institutional rules inside the agent loop makes every compliance change a code change and every code change a compliance review, collapsing two different clocks into one. Separating an authored, versioned policy artifact from a stable runtime lets rules ship at product speed, makes diffs the audit surface, and — critically — means the execution engine stays constant while the constraints move.
article_ideas.title: Policy Is Not a Prompt: Why Rule Changes Shouldn't Be Deploys

article_ideas.angle: Concrete comparison: what an unrolled DAG retry looks like in traces versus a named cyclic node, and which one you can put an eval gate on.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers building orchestration layers, data-platform teams coming from Airflow-style task graphs
article_ideas.based_on: the orchestration substrate needs loop semantics
article_ideas.thesis: Draft-check-refine is a cycle, and forcing it into a directed acyclic graph doesn't remove the loop — it just hides the iteration in re-submitted pipeline runs, unrolled retries, or a single opaque agent call. The cost shows up as invisible latency, unattributable eval regressions, and no place to attach a termination budget. Model the cycle explicitly and give it a name, a budget, and an exit condition.
article_ideas.title: Your DAG Is Lying About Your Refine Loop

evidence_quotes.text: Policies serve as the original institutional intent or system prompt, defining the rules for how work gets done and ensuring risk and compliance adherence.
Build-state and run-state must be separated as two different moments in time.
Allows rapid product updates without breaking core organizational compliance.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent operating under organizational rules needs a policy layer whose lifecycle is decoupled from the execution layer; otherwise every rule change becomes a code change and every code change becomes a compliance review.
core_insights.insight: Split the system into two temporally distinct states: a build-state where policy (institutional intent, the 'system prompt') is authored and revised, and a run-state where execution happens continuously. Policy is a versioned artifact owned outside the runtime, not code embedded in the agent loop.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is the boundary that lets compliance/rules change at product velocity without redeploying or re-validating the execution engine, and it gives a natural diff/audit surface for governance review. It also implies the runtime must read policy as configuration/data at invocation time rather than compile it in.

evidence_quotes.text: Start supervised with every output reviewed by humans.
Sample outputs as confidence scores cross policy thresholds.
Transition to humans handling exceptions only once high confidence is established.
Moving from 0.70 confidence threshold checking every output to 0.90 threshold with sampling and exception handling.

core_insights.generalization: Treat human oversight as a dialed resource allocated proportionally to measured uncertainty, not as a phase you exit; the same pattern applies to auto-retry rates, cache trust, and canary traffic.
core_insights.insight: Autonomy is granted as a graded, measurable ladder rather than a binary decision: run 100% human review on every output, then move to statistical sampling once the confidence score crosses a policy-defined threshold, then move to exception-only human handling. The confidence metric is an operational control input that directly sets the human review fraction — it is not just a dashboard number.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Engineers typically treat the supervised/unsupervised choice as a launch-day switch or as per-task trust. Making the review fraction a function of a measured confidence score converts a judgment call into a tunable controller with an explicit, auditable ramp, and it bounds the blast radius of early errors.

evidence_quotes.text: Probabilistic agents require new evaluation techniques beyond exact output comparison.
Datasets and evals together build confidence in agent outputs.
Evaluating probabilistic outputs requires statistical volume and repeatable test runs rather than single test cases.

core_insights.generalization: Any component whose output distribution is non-degenerate needs a statistical acceptance criterion, and the eval suite must be sized to produce a usable confidence interval rather than a binary verdict.
core_insights.insight: For probabilistic components, unit tests are replaced as the confidence mechanism by representative datasets plus repeated statistical evals over runtime traces — confidence is established through volume and repeatability, not exact-output assertions.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This changes what a 'passing build' means: a single green run carries almost no information about a stochastic agent, so the harness must be built to run N repetitions of a case set and report a distribution, and traces must be captured as first-class eval inputs from production rather than discarded after debugging.

evidence_quotes.text: Workflows can be represented as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) or Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs).
Apache Airflow as an example of a workflow engine representing DAGs in Python code.
Workflows must account for exception paths and feedback loops rather than strict linear progression.
Enables parallel reviews and clear operational visibility into bottlenecks.

core_insights.generalization: When the unit of work is an agent that must self-correct, the orchestration substrate needs loop semantics (with budgets and exit conditions), which is a different primitive than task-graph execution.
core_insights.insight: Agent workflows cannot always be modeled as DAGs: refinement loops (draft → check → refine) require directed cyclic graphs, and the graph representation is what makes parallelism, dependency order, and exception paths explicit.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Choosing DAG-only orchestration forces you to fake iteration with re-submission or unrolled retries, which hides the loop from observability and inflates cost/latency tracking. Explicit cycles make the refine loop a named, bounded, inspectable step with its own termination condition.

evidence_quotes.text: Deterministic outside, adaptive inside.
Quality requires evaluation mechanisms that complement traditional software testing.

core_insights.generalization: Reliability in stochastic systems comes from pushing nondeterminism into the smallest possible region with the tightest typed interface.
core_insights.insight: 'Deterministic outside, adaptive inside': keep the surrounding harness — policy enforcement, graph control flow, thresholds, review routing, exception handling — deterministic and testable with ordinary software engineering, and confine the probabilistic behavior to the inner decision steps.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It tells you where to put the boundary so that failures are attributable: if control flow is deterministic, an eval regression can be blamed on the model step rather than on the orchestrator, and the orchestrator can be unit-tested normally. It also means the safety properties (what must never happen) live in code you can reason about, not in the model.

evidence_quotes.text: Language such as 'must', 'may', and 'should' defines requirement levels.

core_insights.generalization: Normative text with deontic markers can be compiled into tiered runtime controls rather than flattened into a prompt, giving a single source of truth for enforcement severity.
core_insights.insight: Policy language already encodes graded obligation levels ('must', 'may', 'should'), which is a latent machine-readable signal for enforcement strength: hard block, permitted-with-review, or advisory. (Inference: the summary states requirement levels exist but does not say they are enforced programmatically.)
core_insights.why_it_matters: If obligation modality maps to enforcement action, one policy artifact can generate both the agent's instructions and its guardrail configuration, eliminating drift between the written rule and the runtime check — and it gives a principled default for what routes to human review versus what is rejected outright.

evidence_quotes.text: Start supervised with every output reviewed by humans.
Sample outputs as confidence scores cross policy thresholds.

deep_dives.research_question: If the confidence score directly sets the review fraction (100% → sampling → exception-only), what calibration procedure and drift detector keep the earned autonomy level honest across model versions, prompt changes, and shifting input distributions — and what triggers automatic de-escalation back down the ladder?
deep_dives.topic: Calibrating and monitoring a confidence metric that controls the human review fraction
deep_dives.trigger_insight: The confidence metric is an operational control input
deep_dives.why: The entire hill-climbing scheme is only as safe as the scorer's calibration. A silently drifting scorer promotes the agent past a threshold it has not earned, and once oversight is exception-only there is almost no inspection surface left to notice. This converts the scorer from a reporting artifact into the most safety-critical component in the system, and it is currently specified with illustrative numbers (0.70, 0.90) rather than a derivation.

evidence_quotes.text: Language such as 'must', 'may', and 'should' defines requirement levels.
Policies serve as the original institutional intent or system prompt, defining the rules for how work gets done and ensuring risk and compliance adherence.

deep_dives.research_question: Can graded obligation language in a policy artifact be deterministically compiled into enforcement tiers — hard block, permitted-with-review, advisory — such that one policy source generates both the agent's instructions and its guardrail configuration, and does that coupling eliminate drift between the written rule and the runtime check?
deep_dives.topic: Compiling deontic modality ('must'/'may'/'should') into tiered runtime enforcement
deep_dives.trigger_insight: which is a latent machine-readable signal for enforcement strength
deep_dives.why: If it works, policy authorship becomes the single source of truth for enforcement severity and gives a principled default for routing decisions (reject vs. human review vs. log-only) instead of ad-hoc thresholds. If it does not work, we learn where natural-language obligation is too ambiguous to compile and needs human-in-the-loop authoring — both outcomes are actionable. This is explicitly flagged in pass 1 as inference, not a stated claim, so it is a genuine research gap.

evidence_quotes.text: Probabilistic agents require new evaluation techniques beyond exact output comparison.
Datasets and evals together build confidence in agent outputs.

deep_dives.research_question: How many repeated runs per test case are required before an eval verdict on a probabilistic agent is stable enough to gate an autonomy step, and how does that repetition count scale eval cost and wall-clock time against the review labor it replaces?
deep_dives.topic: Sizing the statistical eval harness: repetitions, confidence intervals, and cost
deep_dives.trigger_insight: confidence is established through volume and repeatability
deep_dives.why: A single green run carries almost no information about a stochastic component, so 'passing build' has to be redefined as a distributional claim. Without a stated repetition count and an acceptance criterion expressed as a confidence interval, teams will either under-run evals and ship noise or over-run them and price the harness out of CI. This is directly tied to a key claim flagged as needing verification.

evidence_quotes.text: Workflows can be represented as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) or Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs).
Code review refinement loops where drafts are checked and refined iteratively.

deep_dives.research_question: What is the minimal cyclic-graph primitive (named loop node, iteration budget, explicit termination condition, per-iteration trace span) that supports draft-check-refine cycles without unbounded cost or latency, and does it preserve per-node eval attribution when the same node executes repeatedly?
deep_dives.topic: Loop primitives for agent orchestration: budgets, exit conditions, and per-node attribution
deep_dives.trigger_insight: the orchestration substrate needs loop semantics
deep_dives.why: DAG-only substrates force iteration to be faked via re-submission or unrolled retries, which hides the loop from observability and inflates cost tracking. But adding cycles introduces non-termination risk and makes it hard to attribute an eval regression to a specific step. The tradeoff needs a concrete primitive, not just the observation that cycles exist.

evidence_quotes.text: Build-state and run-state must be separated as two different moments in time.
Policies serve as the original institutional intent or system prompt, defining the rules for how work gets done and ensuring risk and compliance adherence.

deep_dives.research_question: Holding the policy artifact fixed, how much does adherence to each individual policy clause change when the composition of the agent's context window (retrieved documents, tool outputs, conversation history length) is ablated, and is that degradation attributable to specific clause types?
deep_dives.topic: Policy compliance as a property of the (policy, context) pair
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Policy is a versioned artifact owned outside the runtime
deep_dives.why: The build-state/run-state split stabilizes the policy text but not the context it competes with for model attention. If adherence is context-sensitive, then a policy artifact that passed review at build-state can silently violate itself at run-state with no diff to review — a governance failure mode that no amount of policy versioning catches.

project_ideas.based_on: The confidence metric is an operational control input
project_ideas.hypothesis: A per-node calibrated confidence gate with drift detection keeps error escape rate within a fixed tolerance while cutting human review volume substantially versus fixed-rate sampling — and detects scorer drift before error escape rate rises, enabling automatic de-escalation to a higher review fraction.
project_ideas.measurement: Error escape rate as a function of review fraction across thresholds; detection latency between induced drift and the de-escalation trigger; review hours saved at matched escape rate versus a fixed 20% sampling baseline.
project_ideas.name: Autonomy Governor
project_ideas.poc: Wrap a policy-driven workflow (e.g. a document/decision triage step) in a controller that takes a confidence score and outputs a review fraction. Instrument with a labeled holdout set to measure escape rate at each oversight level, plus a drift monitor on the score distribution. Include a de-escalation path that widens sampling when drift is detected.

project_ideas.based_on: which is a latent machine-readable signal for enforcement strength
project_ideas.hypothesis: Deontic markers in policy text can be compiled into enforcement tiers (hard block / permitted-with-review / advisory) that agree with human compliance reviewers' own tier assignments at a high rate, and the compiled guardrails eliminate the drift that accumulates when the same rule is hand-written into both a prompt and a runtime check.
project_ideas.measurement: Classification agreement (and confusion matrix) versus human-assigned tiers; count and severity of prompt-vs-guardrail mismatches before and after compiling from a single source.
project_ideas.name: Modality-to-Guardrail Compiler
project_ideas.poc: Parse a corpus of real policy clauses, classify modality and map to enforcement tier, emit both an instruction fragment for the agent and a runtime guardrail config from the same source. Diff against tiers assigned independently by human reviewers; run a drift audit comparing prompt text and guardrail config in a hand-maintained system.

project_ideas.based_on: confidence is established through volume and repeatability
project_ideas.hypothesis: There is a stable, measurable repetition count per test case beyond which eval verdicts stop flipping across reruns, and that count — not a hand-picked N — should set the CI gate; below it, verdict instability dominates the signal and 'passing' is noise.
project_ideas.measurement: Verdict flip rate and CI width versus N; compute cost per eval run at the chosen N; false-promote rate for autonomy gates when N is set below the knee versus at it.
project_ideas.name: Repetition-Count Harness for Stochastic Evals
project_ideas.poc: Build a harness that runs a fixed case set N times per case and reports per-case pass-rate distributions, verdict-flip rate as N increases, and cost/latency per N. Sweep N across a range and identify the knee where verdict stability converges.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Evan Kormos
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Trusting agents in policy-driven workflows
  • Purpose: Provide a practical framework for enterprise software engineers and managers on how to build trust, establish governance, and evaluate quality when deploying probabilistic AI agents in policy-driven business workflows. Evan Kormos from Coinbase discusses how to safely integrate AI agents into enterprise workflows by establishing clear policies, separating build-state from run-state, structuring workflows as directed acyclic and cyclic graphs, and implementing hill-climbing quality evaluation loops to transition from fully supervised to autonomous operations.

Topic Map

Starting with Policy

  • Explanation: Policies serve as the original institutional intent or system prompt, defining the rules for how work gets done and ensuring risk and compliance adherence.
  • Key claims:
    • Policy represents institutional intent and sets the rules for work.
    • Language such as 'must', 'may', and 'should' defines requirement levels.
    • Build-state and run-state must be separated as two different moments in time.
  • Examples:
    • Defining rules for commercial lending or token listing.
  • Terminology:
    • policy
    • build state
    • run state
    • institutional intent
  • Why it matters: Clear policies provide the necessary boundaries before agents are introduced into organizational workflows.

Agents Meet Process

  • Explanation: Agents operate across the enterprise layers of people, process, and technology by working alongside people, executing parts of the process, and using technology.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents cut across people, process, and technology layers.
    • Workflows can be represented as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) or Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs).
  • Examples:
    • Apache Airflow as an example of a workflow engine representing DAGs in Python code.
  • Terminology:
    • DAG
    • DCG
    • Apache Airflow
    • workflow
  • Why it matters: Mapping workflows as graphs helps engineers understand step dependencies, parallelism, and exception paths.

Quality and Evaluation

  • Explanation: Unlike deterministic software tested with unit tests, probabilistic agents require representative datasets and statistical evals across traces to build confidence.
  • Key claims:
    • Probabilistic agents require new evaluation techniques beyond exact output comparison.
    • Datasets and evals together build confidence in agent outputs.
    • Quality is a team sport involving people, process, and technology.
  • Examples:
    • Code review refinement loops where drafts are checked and refined iteratively.
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • datasets
    • traces
    • confidence mechanism
  • Why it matters: Evaluating probabilistic outputs requires statistical volume and repeatable test runs rather than single test cases.

Turning It On (Hill-Climbing)

  • Explanation: Deploying agents involves starting fully supervised on every output, sampling as confidence climbs, and eventually handling only exceptions through human oversight.
  • Key claims:
    • Start supervised with every output reviewed by humans.
    • Sample outputs as confidence scores cross policy thresholds.
    • Transition to humans handling exceptions only once high confidence is established.
  • Examples:
    • Moving from 0.70 confidence threshold checking every output to 0.90 threshold with sampling and exception handling.
  • Terminology:
    • hill climbing
    • confidence threshold
    • sampling
    • exception handling
  • Why it matters: A gradual ramp-up ensures safety and trust before letting agents run unsupervised.

Key Points

Separate policy from the running system

  • Explanation: Policies are authored and updated in build-state, while systems execute continuously in run-state.
  • Evidence: Distinction between build-state configuration and run-state execution.
  • Practical implication: Allows rapid product updates without breaking core organizational compliance.

Workflows as Directed Graphs

  • Explanation: Workflows should be modeled as DAGs or DCGs to manage dependencies and enable parallel reviews.
  • Evidence: Mention of Apache Airflow and LangGraph for graph state management.
  • Practical implication: Enables parallel reviews and clear operational visibility into bottlenecks.

Confidence through Evals and Datasets

  • Explanation: Traditional unit tests are insufficient for probabilistic AI; instead, use representative datasets and repeated statistical evals.
  • Evidence: Comparison of traditional unit tests with agent eval datasets and runtime traces.
  • Practical implication: Provides statistical confidence in agent outputs rather than binary pass/fail results.

Hill-Climbing Adoption Strategy

  • Explanation: Begin with 100% human supervision and gradually decrease human intervention as agent confidence metrics cross thresholds.
  • Evidence: Graph showing confidence rising from 0.70 (every output) to sampled, and finally 0.90 (exceptions only).
  • Practical implication: Safely reduces operational overhead over time while maintaining high quality.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Hill-Climbing Adoption Framework

  • How it works: Start with full human supervision, measure confidence via evals, increase autonomy and sample outputs as confidence crosses policy thresholds, and finish with humans handling only exceptions.
  • Components:
    • Supervised baseline
    • Confidence measurement
    • Sampling threshold
    • Exception-only human fallback
  • When to use: When transitioning probabilistic AI agents from experimental deployments to unsupervised production workflows.

Examples & Case Studies

A code review workflow featuring a draft-check-refine loop.

  • Illustrates: How directed cyclic graphs (DCGs) handle iterative refinement before passing outputs downstream.
  • Lesson: Workflows must account for exception paths and feedback loops rather than strict linear progression.

Commercial lending and token listing processes modeled as DAGs.

  • Illustrates: Applying policy-driven workflows to regulated financial and cryptographic asset environments.
  • Lesson: Complex enterprise processes can be safely managed by combining human judgment and agent automation.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Separate policy definitions from execution engines.
    • Model workflows as directed graphs (DAGs or DCGs).
    • Implement statistical evals and tracing alongside test datasets.
  • Strategic:
    • Deterministic outside, adaptive inside.
    • Quality requires evaluation mechanisms that complement traditional software testing.
    • AI agents accelerate operations across people, process, and technology.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we define what 'good' looks like for probabilistic agent outputs?
    • At what confidence threshold should we transition from sampling to exception-only human review?
    • How do we maintain policy compliance when agent context windows shift?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Higher quality inputs result in better outputs at a lower compute cost. (empirical)
  • Combining representative datasets and eval traces builds necessary confidence for probabilistic systems. (architectural)

Notable Quotes

"Start with the policy, and it's pretty boring." "Deterministic outside. Adaptive inside." "Quality is a team sport."

Compressed Summary

  • Establish clear written policies before deploying agents.
  • Separate build-state policy definition from run-state execution.
  • Use DAGs and DCGs to structure and parallelize workflows.
  • Build confidence in probabilistic agents using representative datasets, evals, and runtime traces.
  • Adopt a hill-climbing strategy moving from full human supervision to exception-only oversight.
  • Keywords: agents, workflows, policy, evaluation, governance
  • Core insight: Trusting AI agents in policy-driven workflows requires deterministic outer governance coupled with adaptive internal agent loops, verified through rigorous statistical evaluation and hill-climbing adoption.

- **Why it matters**: Clear policies provide the necessary boundaries before agents are introduced into organizational workflows.
### Agents Meet Process
- **Explanation**: Agents operate across the enterprise layers of people, process, and technology by working alongside people, executing parts of the process, and using technology.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents cut across people, process, and technology layers.
  - Workflows can be represented as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) or Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs).
- **Examples**:
  - Apache Airflow as an example of a workflow engine representing DAGs in Python code.
- **Terminology**:
  - DAG
  - DCG
  - Apache Airflow
  - workflow
- **Why it matters**: Mapping workflows as graphs helps engineers understand step dependencies, parallelism, and exception paths.
### Quality and Evaluation
- **Explanation**: Unlike deterministic software tested with unit tests, probabilistic agents require representative datasets and statistical evals across traces to build confidence.
- **Key claims**:
  - Probabilistic agents require new evaluation techniques beyond exact output comparison.
  - Datasets and evals together build confidence in agent outputs.
  - Quality is a team sport involving people, process, and technology.
- **Examples**:
  - Code review refinement loops where drafts are checked and refined iteratively.
- **Terminology**:
  - evals
  - datasets
  - traces
  - confidence mechanism
- **Why it matters**: Evaluating probabilistic outputs requires statistical volume and repeatable test runs rather than single test cases.
### Turning It On (Hill-Climbing)
- **Explanation**: Deploying agents involves starting fully supervised on every output, sampling as confidence climbs, and eventually handling only exceptions through human oversight.
- **Key claims**:
  - Start supervised with every output reviewed by humans.
  - Sample outputs as confidence scores cross policy thresholds.
  - Transition to humans handling exceptions only once high confidence is established.
- **Examples**:
  - Moving from 0.70 confidence threshold checking every output to 0.90 threshold with sampling and exception handling.
- **Terminology**:
  - hill climbing
  - confidence threshold
  - sampling
  - exception handling
- **Why it matters**: A gradual ramp-up ensures safety and trust before letting agents run unsupervised.
## Key Points
### Separate policy from the running system
- **Explanation**: Policies are authored and updated in build-state, while systems execute continuously in run-state.
- **Evidence**: Distinction between build-state configuration and run-state execution.
- **Practical implication**: Allows rapid product updates without breaking core organizational compliance.
### Workflows as Directed Graphs
- **Explanation**: Workflows should be modeled as DAGs or DCGs to manage dependencies and enable parallel reviews.
- **Evidence**: Mention of Apache Airflow and LangGraph for graph state management.
- **Practical implication**: Enables parallel reviews and clear operational visibility into bottlenecks.
### Confidence through Evals and Datasets
- **Explanation**: Traditional unit tests are insufficient for probabilistic AI; instead, use representative datasets and repeated statistical evals.
- **Evidence**: Comparison of traditional unit tests with agent eval datasets and runtime traces.
- **Practical implication**: Provides statistical confidence in agent outputs rather than binary pass/fail results.
### Hill-Climbing Adoption Strategy
- **Explanation**: Begin with 100% human supervision and gradually decrease human intervention as agent confidence metrics cross thresholds.
- **Evidence**: Graph showing confidence rising from 0.70 (every output) to sampled, and finally 0.90 (exceptions only).
- **Practical implication**: Safely reduces operational overhead over time while maintaining high quality.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Hill-Climbing Adoption Framework
- **How it works**: Start with full human supervision, measure confidence via evals, increase autonomy and sample outputs as confidence crosses policy thresholds, and finish with humans handling only exceptions.
- **Components**:
  - Supervised baseline
  - Confidence measurement
  - Sampling threshold
  - Exception-only human fallback
- **When to use**: When transitioning probabilistic AI agents from experimental deployments to unsupervised production workflows.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A code review workflow featuring a draft-check-refine loop.
- **Illustrates**: How directed cyclic graphs (DCGs) handle iterative refinement before passing outputs downstream.
- **Lesson**: Workflows must account for exception paths and feedback loops rather than strict linear progression.
### Commercial lending and token listing processes modeled as DAGs.
- **Illustrates**: Applying policy-driven workflows to regulated financial and cryptographic asset environments.
- **Lesson**: Complex enterprise processes can be safely managed by combining human judgment and agent automation.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Separate policy definitions from execution engines.
  - Model workflows as directed graphs (DAGs or DCGs).
  - Implement statistical evals and tracing alongside test datasets.
- **Strategic**:
  - Deterministic outside, adaptive inside.
  - Quality requires evaluation mechanisms that complement traditional software testing.
  - AI agents accelerate operations across people, process, and technology.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we define what 'good' looks like for probabilistic agent outputs?
  - At what confidence threshold should we transition from sampling to exception-only human review?
  - How do we maintain policy compliance when agent context windows shift?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Higher quality inputs result in better outputs at a lower compute cost. (empirical)
- Combining representative datasets and eval traces builds necessary confidence for probabilistic systems. (architectural)
## Notable Quotes
> "Start with the policy, and it's pretty boring."
> "Deterministic outside. Adaptive inside."
> "Quality is a team sport."
## Compressed Summary
- Establish clear written policies before deploying agents.
- Separate build-state policy definition from run-state execution.
- Use DAGs and DCGs to structure and parallelize workflows.
- Build confidence in probabilistic agents using representative datasets, evals, and runtime traces.
- Adopt a hill-climbing strategy moving from full human supervision to exception-only oversight.
- **Keywords**: agents, workflows, policy, evaluation, governance
- **Core insight**: Trusting AI agents in policy-driven workflows requires deterministic outer governance coupled with adaptive internal agent loops, verified through rigorous statistical evaluation and hill-climbing adoption.
